strengths: The combination of Gaussian affine optimal transport and a normalized Wasserstein residual is an interesting approach to studying activation behavior. Exact recovery under nonsingular positive-definite affine transformations provides a useful, restricted theoretical foundation.

The empirical survey covers many influential convolutional and transformer architectures using all 50,000 ImageNet validation images. The raw signatures and clustering reveal informative patterns, including residual networks’ bimodal profiles and transformers’ lower activation affinity.

The plain-versus-residual network comparison in Figure 5 provides a useful controlled experiment. The additional analyses of initialization, training, and self-supervised checkpoints extend the contribution beyond a catalog of architectures.

Appendix E addresses practical covariance estimation and reports batch-size and nine-seed stability checks. Clear explanatory figures and a supplied code link also support accessibility and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a general nonlinearity measure is not established. Equation (5) compares marginal distributions and discards input-output correspondence. For X uniform on [-1,1] and σ(X)=|X|, the affine map is T_aff(X)=(X+1)/2; both outputs are uniform on [0,1], giving affinity 1 despite σ being nonlinear. The restricted affine theorem does not resolve this identifiability problem. A monotonicity/convex-gradient restriction could help, but GELU and SiLU, which are studied here, have negative-derivative regions. The claimed interpretation of affinity 0 as independence also does not follow from a distance between marginals.

The practical signature is insufficiently connected to the measured network activations. Definition 3.1 uses σ(r(X)), whereas pooling actual activation outputs produces r(σ(X)); these are generally different. For example, averaging ReLU([1,-1]) gives 0.5, while applying ReLU after averaging gives 0. Appendix E’s claim that averaging is lossless is not established by its limited comparison. Covariance shrinkage also changes the exact covariance matching used in the theoretical argument, without establishing which guarantees survive.

The architecture-level conclusions exceed what activation-only signatures establish. Figure 10 measures modules such as ReLU, GELU, and SiLU, while attention’s input-dependent products, softmax, and normalization also contribute nonlinearity. Differences in activation type and training conditions are not controlled across families. The observed profiles are useful descriptors, but they do not establish that transformers have greater overall functional nonlinearity or that this explains their accuracy.

The accuracy-prediction evidence is exploratory. Figure 4 selects the best statistic within each family and evaluates the relationship on the same small collection of models, including only five ViTs. The reported ViT R² of 0.974 therefore demonstrates an in-sample association, without held-out prediction, a specified fit-selection procedure, or uncertainty estimates. Claims about predictive usefulness and architectures implicitly optimizing these statistics are consequently under-supported.

The justification against alternatives contains substantive errors. Remark 3.6 describes T_aff as a globally optimal nonlinear map, although it is affine and is optimal between Gaussian approximations. Standard least squares with an intercept has nonnegative in-sample R², so the stated unbounded-negative disadvantage is not inherent to that baseline. Section 3.3 also dismisses Jacobian-based analysis because of ReLU nondifferentiability, although ReLU networks are differentiable almost everywhere. Low correlation with other metrics establishes difference, not superior measurement validity or usefulness.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: the manuscript does not specify the empirical Wasserstein solver or approximation, precise pretrained checkpoint identifiers, and regression-fitting details. These affect the central results. Smaller, readily correctable presentation issues include calling the Gelbrich lower bound an upper bound and contradictory linearity/nonlinearity wording around Figure 3. The recommendation is driven primarily by the unresolved validity of the metric and the evidence supporting its principal claims.
